prize_parts.citation: For the invention and development of optical lattice clocks, bringing frequency and time measurement to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I keep B015 with Katori and Ye. Having read the full first round, the scientific case has not weakened, and two of the objections have been answered on the physics rather than by counting. The overlap objection is met by the magic-wavelength condition: the 2005 comb prize supplied the optical ruler and the 2012 prize concerned control of single quantum systems, but neither gives a way to interrogate thousands of atoms at once with the lattice light shift cancelled, which is what moved stability and systematic uncertainty by orders of magnitude. The credit is the cleanest on the shortlist: Katori's concept and first realisation, Ye's carrying of the strontium clock to the record regime, and independent confirmation in Sr, Yb and Hg laboratories. A citation that names the lattice clock and its realisation at the 10^-18 level, not frequency metrology in general, keeps ion clocks and combs outside the claim. The Tohoku-reported criterion that the prize is for a discovery or invention and the people responsible for the original work fits this configuration closely.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection remains distinctness from the 2005 and 2012 prizes, and I accept that it is a matter of judgement and not a proof. Danielsson-Ulf and Kroll-Stefan are right that B017 opened a new regime of physics and is broader in reach, and that is a legitimate criterion for a discovery prize. Other lattice-clock groups (SYRTE, PTB, NIST, RIKEN) are not carried by two names, and the redefinition of the second is still pending, so one can argue for waiting. I do not find the case that B015 should wait persuasive, since the redefinition is a policy step and not a doubt about the physics, but I record it.

responses.point: Danielsson-Ulf argues that B017 opened a new regime of physics, that the clock refines a quantity already well measured, and that the maturity test applied to B017 should be applied consistently elsewhere.
responses.response: I accept the consistency point and I apply it the same way: I do not count the open pairing mechanism against B017, because the discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states is reproduced in many laboratories. My ordering therefore does not rest on B017 being immature. It rests on credit. For B017 the experimental credit is carried by one group while Yuan Cao, first author of the 2018 papers, and the Dean, Young, Kim and Yazdani groups sit outside the three names, and no citation wording repairs that. For the clock the credit is a clean two-person split. If the committee ranks breadth of impact above clarity of credit, B017 moves ahead, and I would not call that unreasonable. I am not persuaded that a clock is a smaller thing, since it opens tests of constants, relativistic geodesy and dark-matter searches that the previous prizes did not.

responses.point: Eriksson-Olle prefers B051 with Kane, Mele and Molenkamp, arguing the Z2 insulator is a different discovery from the 2016 topological-phase prize and that the clock's payoff is still prospective.
responses.response: I take the distinction between the 2016 theory of topological order and the Z2 insulator in real materials seriously, and as a materials experimentalist I see the HgTe work as a genuine experimental discovery. My difficulty is the same as with B017: the boundary of credit. Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang proposed the HgTe route, Zhang is deceased, and Hasan's 3D ARPES work is a separate experimental achievement that a three-name cap forces out or merges. On prospective payoff I disagree in part. The lattice clock is already used for tests of fundamental constants and for geodesy comparisons, and the redefinition of the second is an administrative step that follows the physics. I rank B051 below B017 and B015 for this year but I would not call it weak.

responses.point: Kroll-Stefan states that the magic-wavelength condition separates the lattice clock from the comb and ion-clock prizes, and also warns that two experimentalists who like instruments should not treat opening agreement as merit.
responses.response: I agree on both. The magic-wavelength argument is the specific element not covered by the 2005 and 2012 prizes, and it is the answer I would give to the chair's first question. I also accept the warning: four first places in the opening round came from members close to atomic physics and microscopy-type instrument work, and I have tried to test B015 against B017 on the physics and on credit and not on the count. Where I would go further than you is on B016, which we both list. Five names for three places forces an arbitrary cut, and I would not move it ahead of B015 or B017.

responses.point: Johansson-Goran is cautious about B017 maturity and credit, and discounts his own first choice B012 because of the 2025 prize and Chalmers proximity.
responses.response: I appreciate the candour on B012 and I agree that a second superconducting-circuit prize this soon needs a distinct justification that I do not see this year. I share the Chalmers connection with him and it does not affect my view of B015, B017 or B051. On B017, we agree on the structure and on the Yuan Cao omission. Where I differ is that you treat the unresolved mechanism as a timing concern and I do not: the discovery is robust and waiting would not improve it. The real problem is attribution, which time will not fix either, so I would not use maturity as the reason to prefer the clock.

responses.point: Pearce-Mark, as chair, asks whether other lattice-clock groups should replace or join Katori and Ye and whether the redefinition of the second is a reason to wait.
responses.response: I would keep the two-name configuration. SYRTE, PTB and NIST groups did important work, but the magic-wavelength concept and the record systematic uncertainty trace to Katori and Ye, and adding a third name would blur the invention without a principled choice among the others. I would record the omission in the committee's reasoning, as you suggest. On the redefinition of the second, I read it as a consequence of the clock work and not a precondition for recognising it.

uncertainties: Whether the committee judges the lattice clock distinct enough from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes, and whether breadth of impact should outweigh clarity of credit.
Priority among competing lattice-clock groups beyond Katori and Ye, which I recall from memory and have not verified independently.
Whether B017 should lead this year if the experimental credit beyond Jarillo-Herrero could be defended in a three-name citation.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict from my profile for B015 or the credited names Katori and Ye, and none for B017 or B051. I share Chalmers with Göran Johansson, whose first opening choice B012 he has himself discounted; I would recuse or flag if Chalmers colleagues were named in that candidate. My exchanges with Japanese universities are general and do not involve the candidates, including Katori's institution as far as my profile documents. No recusal is needed from my side before the final ballot.
